title: Forgiveness: pardon and overlook
hookLine: a father swears to cut off the relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him a question

cards: Abu Bakr had been supporting a poor relative, a man named Mistah. Then a false accusation spread through Medina about Abu Bakr's own daughter, 'A'ishah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

And Mistah was one of those who repeated it. When the Qur'an cleared her name, Abu Bakr made an oath, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: by Allah, I will never spend anything on Mistah again. On its face, a fair oath.
A verse came down about it anyway.

teach.b: The verse is in surah al-Nur. It speaks to people of means who swear off giving to their relatives and the needy.
Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful."
Two verbs, in Arabic wal-ya'fu wal-yasfahu: pardon, and overlook. 'Afw is letting go of what you're owed: the debt, the punishment, the right to get even.

Overlooking goes one step further: not raising it again, not keeping it ready for the next argument. Then the question. The verse doesn't argue that Mistah deserved help, or that the slander was small.

teach.h: DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?
teach.b: It asks Abu Bakr about himself: do you want to be forgiven? His answer, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me. And he went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop.
Notice the order. The wrong was named first; 'A'ishah's innocence was declared in the Qur'an itself.
Pardon came after the truth, not instead of it. The hadith from the humility day, in Sahih Muslim, has a line for this too, in paraphrase: no servant pardons except that Allah increases him in honor.
So 'afw isn't pretending. It's choosing, with the wrong fully seen, to let the debt go, and then to stop bringing it up.

how: Islamic teaching on pardon draws on Qur'an 24:22 and the story of Abu Bakr resuming his support for Mistah, and on the hadith that Allah increases in honor a servant who pardons.

o: pardon: letting go of what you're owed, with the wrong seen
pretending a wrong never happened so things stay calm
waiting for an apology before you will let anything go

p: never to spend on him again
don't you want to be forgiven?

s: the verse says the slander was a small thing
it doesn't. 'A'ishah's innocence was declared first; pardon came after the truth.
Abu Bakr returned to supporting Mistah
yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me, he said, and resumed it (Bukhari).
overlooking means you never admit you were wronged
the wrong is named and seen; overlooking means not bringing it up again.

games.q: you're Abu Bakr. you've sworn never to support Mistah again. a verse asks: don't you want Allah to forgive you? what do you do?
o: keep the oath; he earned it.
say yes, and go back to supporting him.
support him, but remind him of it often.
games.why: he said: yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me, and restored Mistah's support (Bukhari).

practice: Bring to mind one person who owes you something, an apology, money, a fairer word: not the deepest wound you carry, just something you can hold, and name the wrong plainly without shrinking it.
Then hear the verse's question turned toward you, is there anything you hope to be forgiven for, and if you're ready, let one piece of the debt go, maybe not all of it.
If you pray, you can say the verse's last words in your heart: Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.

wordCard.voice: 'Afw. Pardon: letting go of what you're owed, with the wrong fully seen, and then overlooking it, not bringing it up again. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: pardon, letting go of what is owed.

carryVoice: Your line: pardon and overlook. The truth first, then the letting go. See you tomorrow.
